item.title: Zurich Airport: Driverless Self-Driving Shuttles
item.description: Two fully autonomous electric shuttles at Zurich Airport starting in September. First level 4 project, over 15,000 kilometres tested.
item.content:encoded:
## In brief - Zurich Airport: two driverless shuttles from September 2026 - Level 4 automation, 15,000+ km tested in 1.5 years - Operators reskilled from drivers to remote controllers - Pilot project until end of 2026
## Key facts - **What**: First fully autonomous shuttle system in operation - When: Beginning of September 2026 - Where: Zurich Airport, apron - Who: Flughafen Zürich, WeRide, Swissport, Krummen Kerzers - Test: Over 15,000 kilometers in 1.5 years - Duration: Pilot project until end of 2026
Zurich Airport has reached a historic milestone for automated mobility. Two electric shuttles travel the apron completely autonomously, without any driver on board, monitored exclusively by a remote control center.
The first fully autonomous trips, corresponding to level 4 automation, started at the beginning of September 2026. The project was developed in collaboration with WeRide, the specialized technology partner. Before launch, an intensive testing period of one and a half years was necessary, during which the two vehicles traveled over 15,000 kilometers.
Flughafen Zürich expresses satisfaction with the result. Coralie Klaus Boecker, manager of the airport in the innovation sector, emphasizes the strategic importance: 'Gradual automation of vehicles can make an important contribution to airports, given the growing shortage of specialized labor. For us it was therefore essential to develop the necessary foundations promptly.'
### Initial phase and operational expansion
For the first four weeks, the two shuttles will circulate empty on the airport apron. This validation period serves to further test the system under real operational conditions. Subsequently, the vehicles will be used as shuttles for employees on a defined route that does not cross aircraft taxiways, ensuring the safety of airport operations.
The vehicles are managed remotely by operators from partner companies Swissport and Krummen Kerzers. These operators previously traveled on board as professional drivers and have been reskilled for the new role of remote controllers. Their driving expertise has been redirected toward monitoring and remote control of autonomous systems.
Raphael Glaesener, manager of Flughafen Zürich, clarifies the model: 'Automated driving does not mean that people disappear, but that tasks change. In the future, one employee will be able to supervise several buses, making operations more efficient.' The pilot project will continue until the end of 2026. The data collected will lay the foundation for the expansion of autonomous vehicles at the airport. ## Transformation of the Swiss Labour Market
The Zurich Airport project highlights a concrete challenge faced by Swiss companies: a shortage of specialized labour. According to Flughafen Zürich, this deficit represented one of the main obstacles to the adoption of more efficient technologies. Automation does not mean the disappearance of jobs, but rather the transformation of professional roles. The drivers of Swissport and Krummen Kerzers were not laid off, but rather retrained to fill a new position: that of remote control operators.
This transition represents an important model for the Swiss labour market. Rather than reducing employment, the project has created a new professional competence — remote management of autonomous systems — that requires new digital and supervisory skills. For those working in Switzerland in the transport and logistics sector, this evolution signals a concrete trend: the skills required are shifting from manual driving tasks towards monitoring, diagnostics, and remote supervision competencies.
### Professional Retraining and Operational Efficiency
Companies that invest in professional retraining benefit both from a reduction in operational costs and from the preservation of internal human capital. In the case of Zurich Airport, former drivers become supervisors of multiple vehicles simultaneously, significantly increasing overall efficiency. Employees acquire more sophisticated skills, which are typically associated with higher salaries and career progression.
Zurich Airport is recognized as a pioneer for future applications. The pilot project until the end of 2026 will allow the collection of data that will guide the adoption of autonomous vehicles in other strategic Swiss infrastructures — ports, railway stations, warehouses, urban logistics centres.
### International Competitiveness and Sectoral Implications
The digital transformation of transport positions Switzerland as a global leader in logistics innovation and autonomous mobility. Discover job opportunities in the Swiss transport sector to stay updated on the skills required by the market. Companies operating in logistics, freight transport, and urban mobility services will closely monitor the results of the Zurich project to plan their own automation investments in the coming years.
## Recommended tools For an updated estimate, use the [net salary calculator](nav:calculator) and the [CHF-EUR exchange comparator](nav:exchange). ## Timeline and Operational Phase Until the End of 2026
The project follows a well-defined timeline. From the first weeks of September until the end of 2026, operational data will be collected systematically. Every journey, every remote command, every interaction between the autonomous system and the surrounding environment will feed a database that will be used to improve the reliability and safety of vehicles.
By the end of 2026, Zurich Airport will have accumulated concrete experience on: operational reliability in real conditions, interaction between remote operators and autonomous systems, integration with airport security procedures, feedback from users using the shuttles, organizational impact on the staffing structure and actual operating cost savings.
### From Pilot Phase to Expansion in Swiss Transport
Once the pilot project is concluded, the data will lay the groundwork for expansion at the same airport and potentially at other Swiss infrastructures. Freight transport companies, automated warehouse operators, railway stations and urban logistics services will see this experience as a reference for their innovation strategies.
For those working in the transport sector in Switzerland, the message is clear: professional retraining has become a strategic priority. Companies like Swissport and Krummen Kerzers have already demonstrated that the transition from traditional roles to remote supervision roles is feasible and advantageous. Anyone working in this sector should consider acquiring digital and remote supervision skills as an investment in their professional future.
The shortage of specialized labor that drove the project will not disappear — on the contrary, it will continue to drive investments in automation. The Swiss labor market will increasingly move towards higher-level skills (diagnostics, supervision, programming, systems management), with declining demand for routine driving tasks.
### Next Steps for Those Working in Switzerland
If you work in the transport, logistics or mobility sector in Switzerland and wish to understand how these changes could affect your compensation and tax rights, calculate your Swiss salary and taxes to stay informed about deductions and benefits available in your professional situation.

item.title: Ban on Sudanese gold in Switzerland from 10 September
item.description: The Federal Council has blocked the purchase and import of Sudanese gold since 10 September 2026. Alignment with the EU sanctions of 13 July. Impacts for merchants and financial institutions.
item.content:encoded:
## In brief - Prohibited purchase, import and transit of Sudanese gold from 10 September 2026 - Prohibited supply of financial services and chemical products for gold extraction to Sudan - Federal Council aligned with EU sanctions of 13 July 2026
## Key facts - **What**: Prohibition of trade, import and transit of gold originating from Sudan and certain chemical products - When: 10 September 2026 (entry into force) - Where: Switzerland - Who: Federal Council - Regulatory basis: Ordinance establishing measures against Sudan (RU 2026 462) - Alignment: Decision of the European Union of 13 July 2026
### The Federal Council's decision
The Federal Council decided on 9 September 2026 to prohibit the trade of gold originating from Sudan. The measure enters into force on 10 September 2026. The prohibition covers the purchase, import and transit of Sudanese gold, as well as the provision of financial services and the granting of connected financing means. Also prohibited are the sale and supply of certain chemical products destined for Sudan, used for gold extraction and exploitation.
The Executive justified the decision with extreme concern for the humanitarian situation in Sudan. According to available information, gold constitutes an important conflict resource in the ongoing war in the African country. The ordinance establishing measures against Sudan — in force since 2005 — is used to implement United Nations sanctions and, since 2023, also supplementary measures of the European Union.
### Alignment with the European Union
Switzerland thus aligns itself with the decision of the European Union adopted on 13 July 2026, which provided for similar sanctions against trade in gold originating from Sudan. The Federal Council emphasized that alignment with European measures is part of Swiss strategy in the context of international sanctions policies.
From the ordinance against Sudan, there are already in force an embargo on war material, targeted financial sanctions and travel restrictions against 36 persons, organizations and enterprises. These previous measures remain in force and are supplemented by the new restrictions on gold trade. ### Who is affected by the sanctions
The sanctions directly affect precious metals traders, import-export companies, financial institutions and intermediaries operating in the gold sector. Any activity involving the purchase, sale or transit of Sudanese gold becomes illegal as of September 10, 2026. Companies operating in the chemical and industrial sector must verify that their products destined for Sudan are not used for gold extraction or exploitation. If they are, the supply is prohibited.
This restriction is added to the already strict due diligence obligations that apply in Switzerland for the import of gold and other precious metals. These obligations also aim to prevent trade in resources from conflict zones. Switzerland, even before this decision, imposed strict due diligence standards in the precious metals sector.
### Strengthened compliance obligations
Affected companies must document the origin of gold, supply sources and the chain of custody in full. Verifying that suppliers and customers are not subject to sanctions is a mandatory obligation. Those operating in the sector must implement robust internal controls, thorough document verification and may need to resort to specialized consulting to ensure compliance with the new restrictions.
The new sanctions strengthen the due diligence mechanism and make explicit that Sudanese gold is considered a conflict resource according to international community assessments. This entails increased responsibility for those carrying out gold transactions: any violations expose them to significant legal consequences. ### What Enterprises Must Do
If your company operates in the trade of precious metals, financial services or the production of chemicals, you must immediately verify whether your activities involve Sudanese gold or chemical products destined for Sudan. Check your supply contracts, pending orders and ongoing transactions. If you identify issues, you must cease activities by September 10, 2026, when the ban comes into force. Timely verification is essential to avoid involuntary violations of regulations.
### Verification and Documentation
Verify with your suppliers and customers the origin of gold you import or trade. Request complete certificates of origin and supply chain documentation. Consult the official lists of sanctioned entities maintained by federal authorities to ensure your business partners do not appear among the 36 individuals, organizations and companies already covered by previous restrictions.
Implement or strengthen your internal compliance processes: detailed documentation of transactions, systematic supply chain control, updated records of origin. If your business includes provision of financial services, verify that no transactions concern Sudanese gold and that you do not, indirectly, finance operations linked to this resource. The main [Swiss banks and credit institutions](nav:banks) often have departments specialized in compliance with international sanctions.
### Who to Contact and Deadlines
For specific clarifications on compliance with new sanctions, you can contact the federal authorities competent in matters of foreign trade and sanctions. Legal consultants and international compliance experts can help you adapt business processes within required deadlines. Trade associations in the sectors of precious metals trade, financial services and chemistry can also provide support and specific guidelines.
The operational deadline is September 10, 2026. Do not postpone verifications: any violations of the ban expose you to criminal and civil penalties. If you have doubts about compliance with regulations, seek advice before the date of entry into force.

item.title: Family allowances in Svitto: how to claim them
item.description: In the Canton of Svitto, family allowances are a public contribution for parents with children. Find out who is entitled, how to apply and what documents they need.
item.content:encoded:
## In brief - Schaffhausen pays monthly family allowances for each child based on federal law - Amounts and conditions vary by canton according to local legislation - Application with the local compensation fund
## Key facts - What: Monthly public contribution for parents with children - Where: Canton of Schaffhausen - Who: Parents resident and employed in the canton - Right: Subject to income and number of children - Procedure: Application to the local compensation fund
In the Canton of Schaffhausen, as in every Swiss canton, family allowances are paid monthly to parents who meet specific income and residence requirements. The system is based on a federal law that defines general principles, but leaves to the cantons the autonomy to set local amounts and payment procedures.
Every parent who resides or works in Schaffhausen can claim a contribution for each child, up to an age limit established by cantonal legislation. Allowances are divided into two forms: family allowances for children up to approximately sixteen years old, and training allowances for children in apprenticeships or continuing studies.
Cantonal variability is a structural characteristic of the Swiss system. In the Canton of Schaffhausen, monthly amounts, income thresholds and access procedures may differ significantly from other cantons. For this reason, applicants must verify specific details with the competent local fund.
### How the national system works
The Swiss family allowance system is based on a principle of universality: every parent has the right to support, provided they meet income and residence requirements. The territorial compensation fund manages requests, assesses eligibility and pays monthly amounts to beneficiaries.
The application requires submission of a complete tax return and the birth certificate of each child. For a guide on preparing the documentation, consult the [tax return](nav:tax-return) service. The Schaffhausen cantonal fund processes requests and communicates the outcome within the timeframes established by local legislation. ### Who is Entitled to Family Allowances
To access family allowances in the Canton of Schwyz, the applicant must meet some fundamental requirements. First, they must reside in the canton (or work there, if residing in another Swiss canton); secondly, they must have income determined by dependent or independent employment. Swiss cantonal legislation establishes a minimum and maximum income threshold: below a certain gross annual amount, the parent is not eligible; above another amount, the entitlement expires or is reduced.
The system takes into account the family situation: the number of children, the age of each one and, in some cases, the marital status (married, divorced, widowed, single) affect the determination of the total amount.
### Family Allowances and Training Allowances
Swiss legislation distinguishes between two forms of aid:
- Family allowances: paid monthly for children who have not yet reached the age limit established by the canton (generally sixteen years). The amount is identical for all children. - Training allowances: a form of support for children who are following a professional apprenticeship, school education or study course up to a maximum age that varies by canton.
In the Canton of Schwyz, training allowances have an amount higher than standard family allowances, as they aim to support the cost of professional or academic training.
### Non-Cumulative Character and Annual Variability
Swiss federal law provides that the entitlement to family allowances cannot be cumulative for the same child with two employers or in two different cantons. If a parent changes canton during the year, the application must be updated with the new competent fund.
In case of divorced or separated parents, cantonal legislation defines which parent receives the allowance, usually the parent with custody. The amounts of allowances may undergo annual variations for reasons of indexation or revision of income thresholds; it is important to verify the updated details each year at the local fund.
## Useful planning tools To estimate your pension strategy, use the [pension planner](nav:pension) and the [pillar 3 simulator](nav:pillar3). ### How to submit an application in Canton Schwyz
To obtain family allowances in Canton Schwyz, the first step is to identify the competent compensation fund, usually located in the parent's place of residence.
The application must be submitted on an official form provided by the compensation fund itself. In Canton Schwyz, the form is available at the compensation fund's offices, on the official cantonal website, or at the municipal offices of your residence. You must complete the form in all its parts, providing the applicant's personal data, data for each child (name, date of birth, AVS insurance number if available), and determining income (gross annual, as declared in your last [tax return](nav:tax-return)).
### Required documentation
The competent compensation fund typically requires: - Previous year's tax return (extract from the tax declaration) - Birth certificate for each child - Copy of the employment contract or income declaration for self-employed workers - Possible custody certificate (if parents are divorced or separated)
The exact documentation may vary by canton; it is advisable to verify in advance with the competent compensation fund.
### Deadlines and timelines
There are no strict deadlines for submitting the initial application; however, the right to family allowances generally begins in the month following the submission of a complete request. Cantonal compensation funds generally require renewal of documentation every year or every two years, according to their internal rules.
### How to find the compensation fund and updated information
Updated information on amounts, deadlines, and exact procedures in Canton Schwyz are available from the local compensation fund, the canton's municipalities, and the official websites of the cantonal administration. Consulting directly with the compensation fund ensures you receive the most up-to-date and specific information for your personal situation.

item.title: Swiss pension funds: +0.7% in August
item.description: Foreign shares boosted (+14%): UBS analyzes August performance. Social security funds up to 3.3% per year on average since 2006.
item.content:encoded:
## In a nutshell - Average August return 0.7%, positive for Swiss pension funds - Foreign stocks shine (+14%), supported by corporate earnings and AI - Swiss bonds in red (-0.2%); moderate real estate (+2%) - Annual performance since 2006 has reached an average of 3.3%
## Key facts - **What**: Positive performance of Swiss pension funds in August - When: August 2026 (periodic UBS analysis) - Where: Switzerland - Who: UBS (analysis), Swiss pension funds - Amount/Percentage: Average yield 0.7% (net expenses)
Swiss pension funds ended August in positive territory. According to UBS's periodic analysis, the average return of Swiss pension funds in the month stood at 0.7% net of management fees. The figure reflects different dynamics in the various investment classes: particularly bright were foreign stocks (+14.0%), followed by Swiss stocks (+10.2%), while bonds recorded mixed performances and real estate made a modest positive contribution.
Among fixed-income instruments, foreign bonds maintained a positive return of 0.7%, but Swiss bonds closed slightly negative (-0.2%). Properties, traditionally stable in social security portfolios, contributed +2.0%. In the period examined, the best pension fund achieved a return of +3.2%, while the least effective one stopped at 0.0%.
UBS attributes the boost to stocks ### What These Returns Mean for Pension Holders August's positive returns are no academic curiosity for those with capital locked in a Swiss pension fund (LPP/BVG). Every tenth of a percentage point of annual return translates into a more substantial pension annuity, since the capital accumulated during working life contributes directly to the amount of the benefit. A worker who accumulates contributions from age 25 to age 65 depends heavily on the performance of the portfolio in which the fund has invested their capital.
Portfolio composition – how much is allocated to stocks, how much to bonds, how much to real estate – determines volatility and return potential. Understand how the [cost of living in Switzerland](nav:cost-of-living) impacts your pension planning and the returns needed to maintain the same purchasing power. August demonstrated how stocks, especially foreign ones, can deliver significant recoveries in short periods. Swiss stocks (+10.2%) and even more foreign stocks (+14.0%) drove overall performance. In parallel, the negative data for Swiss bonds (-0.2%) reminds us that even fixed-income securities are not immune to market movements. Real estate, with a +2.0%, continues to provide stability to portfolios, albeit with lower returns compared to stocks.
### Impact of Forecasts on Future Investments UBS forecasts that stocks will continue to be supported by robust corporate profits and investments in artificial intelligence. The Federal Reserve is expected to raise interest rates twice: the first in the current month of September and the second in December, in both cases by a quarter point. These movements directly impact pension fund investment strategies, because higher rates make future bonds more attractive, while they can moderate short-term equity growth.
For those accruing benefits in a pension fund, the economic cycle influences the value of the benefit. A phase of rising rates, if accompanied by rising corporate profits (as forecasts suggest), creates a kind of equilibrium: equities maintain support from corporate earnings, while bonds regain appeal for new investors. Learn more about how occupational pensions work with our [LPP/BVG annuity calculator](nav:pension). Pension funds that wisely balance these two components tend to generate stable returns over the medium to long term.
## Useful planning tools To estimate your pension strategy, use the [pension planner](nav:pension) and the [pillar 3 simulator](nav:pillar3). ### Monitor your pension position If you are a salaried employee in Switzerland, part of your salary is paid by your employer into a professional pension fund (LPP/BVG). It is useful to know how this resource is evolving. Most funds issue annual account statements (usually at year-end) that show the accumulated capital, contributions paid during the period, accrued interest, and the estimated pension amount when reaching the legal retirement age.
Checking your fund's performance against market benchmarks helps you understand if the management is efficient. A return significantly below average could signal excessive management costs or investment choices that are too conservative compared to your risk profile. Conversely, a return above average indicates that the fund is seizing market opportunities (such as exposure to equities during recovery moments, as in August).
### What to do right now First: request the latest account statement from your pension fund from your employer or directly from the institution if you have their contact details. The document must show the value of your accumulated capital. Second: compare the reported return with industry averages published by UBS or other independent analysis providers. Specialized sites publish annual rankings of funds by management category.
Third: evaluate the risk profile of your allocation. If you are young and far from retirement, a portfolio more oriented towards equities may be appropriate to leverage growth potential. If you are close to retirement, a more balanced composition between equities and bonds is preferable to reduce volatility. Fourth: contact the fund in case of doubts about the portfolio composition, management fees, or to understand the options for choosing between different investment profiles, if available.
Keep an eye on the Federal Reserve's decisions and global markets: August showed how attention to artificial intelligence and business results can accelerate recoveries in equity markets. Check the impact of pension contributions on your [payslip](nav:payslip) with our specialized calculator.

item.title: Rural Broadband: The Federal 2030-2037 Program
item.description: The Federal Council approves the broadband support programme on 9 September 2026. Investment of 365 million federal CHF to bring fast internet to rural areas.
item.content:encoded:
## In Brief - The Federal Council approves on September 9, 2026 the law on broadband support - Total investment of CHF 730 million (CHF 365 million from the Confederation) - Objective: minimum speed of 1 Gbps download for residences and commercial activities - 8-year program (2030-2037) in sparsely populated areas
## Key Facts - **What**: Federal law on support for broadband expansion (LSBL) - When: Approval on September 9, 2026; program start from 2030 - Where: Sparsely populated areas of Switzerland - Who: Federal Council, Municipalities, Participating Cantons - Amount: CHF 365 million from the Confederation (2030-2037) - Duration: 8 years, renewable only once for a maximum of 3 years - Target speed: At least 1 gigabit per second download
The Federal Council approved on September 9, 2026 the message to Parliament on the broadband support law (LSBL), with the objective of bridging the digital divide between urban and rural areas of Switzerland. The decision responds to the urgent need to expand modern fiber optic and radio communication networks where expansion is not economically convenient for private providers.
According to official estimates, approximately ten percent of Swiss households and commercial activities remain unconnected to modern broadband networks. The gradual phase-out cycle of copper cables, scheduled from 2030 onwards, makes federal intervention even more urgent. Without the support of the Confederation, entire rural municipalities would risk remaining excluded from access to essential digital infrastructure.
### What the Program Provides
The support program aims to guarantee nationwide comprehensive coverage of residential and commercial buildings through fixed connections with transmission speeds of at least 1 gigabit per second download. Priority is given to fiber optic expansion, the fastest and most reliable technology; where costs prove excessive, federal funding also extends to terrestrial radio communication infrastructure.
The total investment amounts to CHF 730 million, with the Confederation providing CHF 365 million. The Confederation requests from the Federal Assembly a commitment credit of CHF 365 million for the years from 2030 to 2037. Financing comes from taxes on future mobile telephony concessions, a choice that avoids placing additional burden on other federal budget items.
The program has a duration of eight years; however, the Federal Council may extend it only once for a maximum of three years should the available funds not be completely exhausted. This temporal flexibility makes it possible to adapt the pace of expansion to the actual availability of resources and to the operational capacity of the municipalities and cantons involved.
### The Role of Municipalities and Cantons
Participation in the program is voluntary for both municipalities and cantons, but canton accession is necessary to unlock federal co-financing. Each participating canton must bear 50% of the total amount to be financed in each individual project; the Confederation covers the other half through the commitment credit of CHF 365 million. Interested municipalities submit their application to their canton of origin. The Confederation has simplified certain administrative aspects on the basis of opinions received during the public consultation phase, reducing bureaucracy for municipalities. ### The implications for the economic and residential fabric
Modern broadband is not just a convenience; it represents a strategic infrastructure that changes the attractiveness of rural areas as places of residence and work. Today, the digital divide amplifies the economic divide between urban centers and peripheral areas. A family considering moving out of the city carefully weighs the local [cost of living](nav:cost-of-living), available job postings, public services, and increasingly, access to a reliable internet connection.
At speeds of 1 gigabit per second, fiber optic broadband enables actual telework, not just theoretical. Professionals, consultants, developers, designers, and administrative employees can work from anywhere in Switzerland, provided they have a stable and fast connection. The federal program recognizes that without public intervention, the private market would not invest in less populated areas, thus perpetuating the economic isolation of these communities.
### How the program reduces the territorial divide
The expansion of broadband to all Swiss municipalities, regardless of population density, aims directly to reduce the divide in [cost of living](nav:cost-of-living) and opportunities between regions. Municipalities that today struggle to attract residents and investments could become more competitive if they offer telecommunications infrastructure comparable to urban areas. The moment is critical: copper cables, currently still in service, will be gradually decommissioned from 2030 onwards. Without intervention, this natural cycle of technological replacement would have resulted in service interruption in rural areas deemed unprofitable by private providers. The program anticipates this process, ensuring that all municipalities have simultaneous access to modern technologies.
### Scenarios of local economic impact
A small rural municipality in Valais, the Jura, or in the outlying areas of central Swiss cantons could, thanks to broadband, see the number of inhabitants choosing telework grow. This would result in an increase in local consumption, stable rents, and improvement in the perceived [cost of living](nav:cost-of-living) in small municipalities. The collection of municipal taxes could increase, and local economic fabric could be revived. Public transport rates could also stabilize, given that fewer people would need to commute daily to urban centers.
On the other hand, urban municipalities of major cities could see narrower margins of territorial growth if their infrastructural advantages diminish. This process of territorial rebalancing is a natural consequence of broadband expansion at the national level. The Federal Council received clear majority support from participants in the public consultation procedure. This reflects widespread recognition among major Swiss stakeholders of the importance of this infrastructure for the country's future.
## Useful tools to protect your net income To reduce FX leakage, compare [CHF-EUR exchange options](nav:exchange) and [banks for cross-border workers](nav:banks). ### How to Participate: Next Steps
If you are a mayor of a rural municipality or a representative of a canton interested in accessing federal funding, it is essential to understand the procedure in detail. Participation is voluntary, but timing is important to maximize implementation within the program's timeframe (2030-2037, potentially extendable until 2040).
The procedure begins at the municipal level: the interested municipality must submit an application to its canton, documenting the area to be covered, the proposed technology (fiber optics or radio communication), and estimated costs. The canton evaluates the application and, if it decides to participate in the program, commits to co-financing 50% of the expenses. The Confederation, through its credit commitment of 365 million francs, covers the other 50%. Financial aid is limited to what is necessary: these are not unlimited subsidies, but contributions calibrated based on actual implementation costs. This mechanism encourages efficiency in project management and reduces waste of public money.
### Official Timeline and Deadlines
The Federal Council approved its message to Parliament on September 9, 2026. The next crucial step is the discussion of the draft law in both chambers of the Federal Assembly (National Council and Council of States). No precise schedule has yet been communicated for parliamentary votes, so municipalities and cantons should prepare now for the operational phase.
The actual program begins on January 1, 2030, and runs through December 31, 2037. During these eight years, the Confederation and cantons will collaborate to finance and implement projects. If funds remain available at the end of the eighth year, the Federal Council may request Parliament to extend the program for a maximum of three years, extending the deadline to December 31, 2040.
### Resources and Official Information
The Confederation has made various documents available on its administrative portal (admin.ch). These include the complete message to Parliament, the text of the draft broadband law (LSBL), and the federal decree regarding the credit commitment for financing 2030-2037. Municipalities and cantons can consult the official website dedicated to the broadband support law to learn more about administrative requirements, application forms (to be published once the law is approved), and contact information for responsible federal authorities.
If you are a resident of a rural area, you can also encourage your municipality or canton to participate in the program. Consult the [cost of living calculator](nav:cost-of-living) in your Swiss region to assess how access to modern broadband could impact your quality of life and remote work opportunities. Contact your municipality to find out whether a broadband expansion project has already been submitted, or if there is interest in doing so once the federal program takes effect in 2030.

item.title: Zimmer Biomet cuts in Winterthur, Unia in the field
item.description: 580 cuts on 730 seats at Zimmer Biomet (Winterthur). The Unia union protests: workers do not have to pay for the enrichment of shareholders.
item.content:encoded:
## In brief - Zimmer Biomet plans 580 job cuts out of 730 positions in Winterthur - Unia demands maintaining a core company for 'Swiss Made' - Cantonal elections in spring: union will assess politicians
## Key Facts - What: Elimination of 580 jobs out of 730 at Zimmer Biomet - Where: Winterthur, canton of Zurich - Who: Zimmer Biomet (orthopedic medical devices), Unia union - Timeline: Consultation ongoing; cantonal elections spring 2027 - Statement: Serge Gnos, co-head of Unia Zurich-Shaffhausen
Zimmer Biomet, a multinational specializing in orthopedic medical devices, has announced the possible elimination of 580 jobs out of 730 at its facility in Winterthur, in the canton of Zurich. The reaction was immediate: the Unia union has called it unacceptable that workers pay the price for enriching anonymous shareholders of a multinational group.
### The shareholders' strategy
Over the past four years, Zimmer Biomet has pursued a consistent strategy aimed at increasing shareholder value through substantial share buybacks and dividend distributions, according to Unia's accusation. The multinational's focus on global profits stands in stark contrast to local employment risks.
The union participated in the ongoing consultation process and proposed an alternative: maintain in Winterthur a sufficiently large core business to allow Zimmer Biomet to continue selling its products as 'Swiss Made' on the global market. This is not merely about preserving jobs, but also about protecting the Swiss quality brand that Zimmer Biomet uses as a competitive advantage.
### The union's voice
Serge Gnos, co-head of Unia Zurich-Shaffhausen, emphasized in an official statement that behind the numbers are people. 580 jobs are not just a figure: behind each number is a person who perhaps has worked at Zimmer Biomet for decades, who supports a family and contributes to the development of Winterthur. Gnos added that this is about livelihoods and futures, not just global multinational profits.
Unia's protest is not limited to local defense. Gnos stated that the organization will assess politicians in the upcoming spring cantonal elections based on their willingness to preserve manufacturing industry in the canton of Zurich. ### The Role of Trade Unions in the Swiss Labor Market
Unia's position reflects the central role that trade unions play in protecting workers' rights in Switzerland. Although the unionization rate varies by sector and canton, organizations like Unia have decision-making power in company consultations and can influence public debate on critical employment issues.
In the case of Zimmer Biomet, the ongoing consultation represents an opportunity for Unia to negotiate alternatives to massive layoffs. The request to maintain a core business unit is not merely symbolic: it reflects awareness that relocating production to countries with lower costs is a common practice among multinational corporations, but that a manufacturing base in Switzerland is essential to maintain expertise, skilled employment, and added value linked to 'Swiss Made'.
### Swiss Made: Beyond Marketing
The 'Swiss Made' brand has concrete implications not only for Zimmer Biomet's marketing, but for the entire Swiss economy. Products labeled as 'Swiss Made' command higher commercial margins in global markets thanks to the perception of quality and precision. If Zimmer Biomet transferred production entirely abroad, it could lose this advantage — or it would need to reimport from foreign subsidiaries and still claim the Swiss brand, which regulations allow only with precise origin requirements.
### The Challenge for the Canton of Zurich
Zimmer Biomet is an industrial company with a long tradition in Winterthur. The planned layoffs place the Canton of Zurich before a choice: passively accept relocation, or negotiate with the multinational to preserve skilled employment and local tax base. Gnos has launched an explicit appeal to the authorities of Winterthur and the Canton of Zurich to mobilize during the ongoing consultation.
The spring cantonal elections will represent a moment of evaluation: how authorities and governments address employment crises will be a determining factor in the judgment of citizens and workers. A worker who remains employed also has pension rights guaranteed through the [company pension fund](nav:pension); those who lose their job must promptly verify the status of their own provisions.
## Useful planning tools To estimate your pension strategy, use the [pension planner](nav:pension) and the [pillar 3 simulator](nav:pillar3). ### What to do as a worker in Switzerland affected by employment crises
If you work in the manufacturing sector or multinational companies in Switzerland, the cuts announced by Zimmer Biomet remind us of the importance of monitoring signals of company stability and knowing your rights.
Union membership: Joining a union organization such as Unia (in the private sector and industry) or other unions relevant to your sector offers protection during restructuring consultations. Unions have access to official processes and can negotiate exit conditions, seniority protection and retraining plans.
Participation in consultations: If your company initiates a consultation process (as in the Zimmer Biomet case), read all distributed documents and participate in information meetings. Company committees and union representatives provide regular updates.
Monitoring benefits and pensions: In case of dismissal in Switzerland, it is essential to verify the status of your company pension fund (LPP/BVG) and unemployment insurance coverage managed by cantonal offices (SECO coordinates federal benefits).
### Retraining opportunities
Many Swiss cantons, including Zurich, offer professional retraining programs funded by unemployment or regional funds. If a company informs you of imminent cuts, contact your cantonal employment office to learn about training paths available in your sector or related sectors. Portals such as [our job opportunities archive](nav:jobs) help map open positions in Switzerland.
### Cantonal elections: your vote counts
As highlighted by Gnos of Unia, the cantonal elections in spring 2027 will be a crucial moment. Evaluate candidates and parties based on their position towards local industry, investments in skilled employment and negotiations with multinationals. Some parties and cantonal governments are more proactive in supporting companies in crisis; others adopt a more free-trade approach.
### Consult local experts
If you work in a company involved in restructuring, do not hesitate to contact your sector union, consult a law firm specializing in Swiss labor law, or verify cantonal regulations on dismissal protection.
To learn more about how to protect your employment rights and better understand personal financial planning in case of unemployment, consult our [salary and tax calculator](nav:calculator) — a useful tool to evaluate income scenarios and plan your financial future.
*Source: [swissinfo.ch](https://www.swissinfo.ch/ita/unia-su-tagli-a-winterthur%2c-%22lavoratori-non-paghino-per-azionisti%22/92031502)*

item.description: Bellinzona, Cantone-Comuni dialogue on tax, Ticino 2020 and ARP reform. At center: abolition of federal rental value and secondary residence tax
item.content:encoded:
## In a nutshell - 77th session of the Canton-Community Dialogue Platform (9 September, Bellinzona) - Focus on tax adjustment after federal rental value abolition - New cantonal tax on secondary residences being defined - Updates on Ticino 2020 and ARP/Preture protection reform
## Key facts - **What**: Canton-Community dialogue platform discusses taxation, projects and reforms - When: 9 September 2026 (Wednesday) - Where: Bellinzona - Who: Council of State, Head of the Local Authorities Section, Municipal representatives - Session number: 77th since the establishment of the Platform - Central theme: Adaptation of the tax system after abolition of federal rental value - Topic 2: Set up secondary residences (working group of experts) - Next meeting: 2 December 2026
The second session of 2026 of the Canton-Community Dialogue Platform, the 77th since its establishment, took place on Wednesday 9 September in Bellinzona. The meeting was attended by the Council of State accompanied by the head of the Local Authorities Section and representatives of the Ticino Municipalities.
The initial discussion saw the Municipalities express their expectations towards the Council of State and the Cantonal Administration. The discussion focused on three issues of strategic importance for the territory: the reorganization of the tax system, the "Ticino 2020" project and the administrative reform of the Regional Protection Authorities.
### The system The Bellinzona meeting reflects how Swiss taxation operates at three distinct levels. At the federal level, the direct federal tax (DFT) operates, managed by the Federal Customs Administration (FCA/ESTV). At the cantonal and municipal level, each territory has its own competence in setting rates and local taxes. In Ticino, the system is administered by the Local Authorities Section, which coordinates with the Municipalities to ensure compliance with federal regulations and consistency of necessary adjustments.
The abolition of imputed rent is a decision by the federal legislature that removes from the taxable base the income imputed to owners of properties where they reside. This change requires Cantons to adapt by modifying their tax systems. Ticino, like other Cantons, must decide how to compensate for any loss of revenue and how to structure the new levy. This is why the expert group is working: to find solutions that maintain the financial balance of Ticino's Municipalities and do not compromise the cost of living in the territory.
### The New Tax on Secondary Residences
The proposal to tax secondary residences at the cantonal level represents an opportunity for new revenue. Anyone who owns a property in Ticino in addition to their primary residence may be subject to this tax. However, the details (rate, taxable base, exemptions) have not yet been communicated. The expert group — composed of representatives from the Canton and the Municipalities — must develop a proposal that is fair and administratively feasible. To better understand the context on taxes and [cost of living in Switzerland](nav:cost-of-living), you can consult dedicated resources.
### The Administrative Reform of Justice
The reform of Regional Protection Authorities (RPA) represents a broader reorganization of cantonal justice. The current RPAs will be replaced by the new Protection Courts, whose creation and organization has already been approved by the Great Council. This transition involves adjustments in structures, personnel, and procedures. The meetings planned in the coming months with current RPA staff serve to ensure an orderly transition and to clarify the details of the new organizational structure.
## Recommended tools For an updated estimate, use the [net salary calculator](nav:calculator) and the [CHF-EUR exchange comparator](nav:exchange). For the Ticino municipalities, the coming months represent a period of waiting and preparation. The fiscal adjustments required by the abolition of the rental value will not have an immediate effect: one must wait for the results of the work of the expert group, the resolutions of the State Council and their communications to local administrations. Monitor the official communications from the Local Entities Section and the Canton to know the precise procedures and deadlines.
Regarding the new tax on secondary residences, the timing is not yet defined. The expert group is still developing the proposal, so a decision is still far away. Owners of second homes in Ticino will have to wait for an official announcement before knowing how the measure will affect them.
### Concrete steps in the coming months
1. **Fiscal group**: Work continues on redefining fiscal policy post-rental value and on the proposal for a tax on secondary residences. A report or proposal is expected by the end of the year or early months of 2027.
2. ARP meetings: Meetings are beginning between the Cantonal Administration and the staff of the current ARP to illustrate the transition path towards the new Protection Preturas.
3. Next Canton-Municipalities meeting: Set for December 2, 2026. It could bring further updates on all three topics (fiscal, Ticino 2020, ARP).
### What you can do right away
If you are a municipal administrator in Ticino, maintain regular contact with the Local Entities Section to receive timely information. If you are an owner of a second home in Ticino, stay updated on cantonal communications regarding the new tax. To better understand the Swiss fiscal system in its three levels (federal, cantonal, municipal) and how taxes are calculated on income and capital, consult the [salary and tax calculator](nav:calculator) for a complete overview of taxation in Switzerland.
*Source: [tio.ch](https://www.tio.ch/ticino/politica/1949079/cantone-e-comuni-si-confrontano-su-fisco-progetto-ticino-2020-e-riforma-arp)*

## In brief - Internships for newly graduated students at the Federal Administration - 50 professional training programs available in various sectors - Benefits: flexible work arrangements, competitive remuneration
## Key facts - **What**: Opportunities for internships, professional training programs and federal careers - Who: Swiss Federal Administration - Opportunities: 50 professional training programs and internships for newly graduated students - Benefits: Flexible work arrangements, performance-based remuneration, continuous training - Environment: Multidisciplinary teams, innovative solutions - Impact: Concrete contribution to the quality of life in Switzerland
The Swiss Federal Administration positions itself as an attractive employer for those intending to start a career in the public sector. The official portal stelle.admin.ch centralizes the offer of internships for newly graduated students, 50 structured professional training programs and flexible employment conditions. The fundamental value of the federal entity is to put its talent at the service of Swiss public interest, working in multidisciplinary teams on innovative solutions. The official communication emphasizes how working at the Federal Administration is meaningful and allows one to take on concrete responsibilities for the well-being of the population.
### Newly graduated students and internship opportunities
The Federal Administration proposes to young graduates a structured internship pathway that combines the acquisition of concrete hands-on experience, expansion of the professional network and direct contribution to projects of national interest. According to the official communication, these internships allow young people to immediately apply the knowledge acquired during their studies to real problems in Switzerland. The 50 professional training programs mentioned span various sectors of the Federal Administration. Although the source does not specify details for each training program, the message emphasizes the commitment to sectors of national relevance such as social policies, economics, environment, justice and security.
### Employment conditions and benefits
The federal employer does not limit itself to promising meaningful employment, but highlights concrete benefits that respond to current labor market needs. The Federal Administration offers three main pillars: flexible work arrangements, performance-based remuneration and continuous training. These measures place the entity among the most attractive employers for Swiss talent, in a context where competition for skills is increasing. Performance-based remuneration, in particular, represents a significant difference compared to more traditional public salary models anchored solely to seniority. For operational details on application deadlines and open positions, it is necessary to consult directly the recruitment portal. ### The Federal Administration's positioning in the national labor market
The Federal Administration is one of Switzerland's major employers, managing a workforce distributed throughout the national territory and operating in very diverse fields: central administration, research, security, social and economic policies. The ability to attract young talents through structured internship programs is crucial for the generational renewal of the federal public sector. The offer of flexible work arrangements responds to a global trend that characterizes the contemporary labor market: new generations of graduates increasingly value the balance between professional life and personal commitments. In the Swiss context, where public salaries are historically competitive, flexibility has become a differentiating element to attract the best candidates. You can compare federal opportunities with the private sector by consulting [job postings](nav:jobs).
### Compensation and career progression
The source explicitly mentions compensation based on performance, an element that distinguishes the federal offer from other public administrations that follow rigid salary grids based on seniority. For those entering as recent graduates, this means that the possibility of increasing your income does not depend solely on automatic advancement through seniority steps, but also on effective contribution to projects and achievement of objectives. Continuous training represents a direct investment by the institution in the professional growth of its staff. In a context of digital transformation of public administration and growing national challenges (environmental sustainability, data governance, advanced social policies), the ability to update skills is a fundamental added value for those working in federal institutions.
### Where to look and how to orient yourself
Anyone interested in working for the Federal Administration must access the official portal stelle.admin.ch, which centralizes information on internships, professional training and job postings. This portal is the official tool for knowing application deadlines, specific requirements for each position and details on the training offered. The diversity of 50 training programs suggests that the Federal Administration covers a broad range of professional profiles, not only administrative and managerial, but probably also technical, scientific and specialized. Without access to disaggregated data from stelle.admin.ch, it is difficult to establish which sector has the greatest demand for personnel in the coming period.
## Useful planning tools To estimate your pension strategy, use the [pension planner](nav:pension) and the [pillar 3 simulator](nav:pillar3). ### How to Apply to Federal Administration: Basic Procedure
The first step to explore opportunities with the Federal Administration is to visit the official portal stelle.admin.ch, where all information about apprenticeships, professional training programs, and job postings is centralized. Here you can filter opportunities by sector of interest.
The application procedure follows these essential steps:
1. Access the stelle.admin.ch portal and navigate to the apprenticeship or training section of interest 2. Verify specific requirements: university degree, required certifications, language skills, specific experience 3. Prepare a complete application: curriculum vitae, cover letter, academic or professional references 4. Submit your application online respecting the deadlines indicated in the selection notice 5. Wait for contact from the entity for any selection interviews or subsequent evaluations
### What to Expect from a Federal Apprenticeship
If selected for an apprenticeship, the recent graduate gains access to a structured experience that combines operational duties with integration into multidisciplinary teams. During the apprenticeship, the candidate has access to complementary training directly during the performance of the assignment, thus accelerating the acquisition of practical skills. The duration and specific compensation of apprenticeships are not detailed in the official portal communication, but federal apprenticeships historically represent an entry point to the federal public sector, often a precursor to stable employment positions. The 50 professional training programs mentioned follow paths for acquiring specialized skills, potentially over multiple years, with the issuance of certifications recognized at the federal level.
### Next Steps: Evaluate Economic Impact and Compare Opportunities
Anyone already working in Switzerland and wishing to assess how a career with the Federal Administration would impact personal economic aspects (taxes, social security contributions AVS/LPP, social benefits) can use the [salary calculators](nav:calculator) available to simulate net income scenarios with a federal salary. This is particularly useful for those undecided between a private sector career and federal employment, as it allows you to evaluate the net economic advantage beyond the benefits of flexibility and job stability offered by the public entity. Consult [job postings](nav:jobs) for a broader view of employment opportunities in Switzerland and to compare federal positions with the private market.

item.title: Issuance of federal loans: CHF 368.6 billion
item.description: The Swiss Confederation issued two federal loans on 9 September 2026: CHF 161.240 million at 0.875% until June 2041, and CHF 207.390 million at 0.5% until May 2058. Total volume of CHF 368.630 million.
item.content:encoded:
## In Brief - Confederation issues two loans on 9 September 2026 for CHF 368,630 million - First loan: 0.875% until 24 June 2041; second: 0.5% until 30 May 2058 - Exceptional demand: coverage at 138% and 168% respectively - Release scheduled for 23 September 2026
## Key Facts - **What**: Issuance of two Swiss federal loans through auction procedure - When: 9 September 2026; settlement 23 September 2026 - Where: Swiss Confederation (managed by Federal Finance Office) - Who: Swiss federal administration - Total amount: CHF 368,630 million - Interest rates: 0.875% (first loan) and 0.5% (second loan) - Maturity dates: 24 June 2041 and 30 May 2058
The Swiss Confederation issued two loans through an auction procedure on 9 September 2026, for a total amount of CHF 368,630 million. This is an ordinary financing operation of the Confederation, managed by the Federal Finance Office (EFV), which allows the federal administration to finance itself on international markets at favorable conditions.
### First Loan: 0.875% until June 2041
The first loan has an interest rate of 0.875% and matures on 24 June 2041. The issued amount is CHF 161,240 million, at an issuance price of 103.95%, corresponding to an annual yield of 0.595%. The loan recorded total subscriptions of CHF 223,240 million, with a coverage ratio of 138% (demand exceeding supply). Allocations at the lowest price tier reached 100%, while non-price-indicated bids amounted to CHF 112,940 million. This loan will be settled on 23 September 2026 and has been assigned the provisional ISIN CH1544304137, and is fungible with ISIN CH1544304103.
### Second Loan: 0.5% until May 2058
The second loan has an interest rate of 0.5% and matures on 30 May 2058. The issued amount is CHF 207,390 million, at an issuance price of 98.25%, with an annual yield of 0.560%. This ultra-long-term loan recorded total subscriptions of CHF 349,090 million, with a coverage ratio of 168%, highlighting strong market demand. Allocations at the lowest price tier reached 100%, with non-price-indicated bids of CHF 52,740 million. This loan will also be settled on 23 September 2026 and has received the provisional ISIN CH1544304145, fungible with CH0224397338.
### High Market Demand
The exceptional coverage ratios (138% for the first loan, 168% for the second) indicate that demand significantly exceeded supply. This positive signal reflects the international attractiveness of Swiss government securities, considered among the safest investments in the world thanks to the Confederation's AAA rating. Legal restrictions on these loans can be viewed through the Federal Finance Office portal. ## Economic context and significance of interest rates
Interest rates on Swiss federal loans reflect the economic strength of the Confederation and the decisions of the Swiss National Bank (SNB) regarding monetary policy. The 0.875% of the first loan offers a modest but stable return for those investing in government bonds over the medium to long term (15 years), while the 0.5% of the second represents an ultra-long-term financing source over 32 years, typically intended to cover federal infrastructure projects with a very long time horizon.
The difference between the stated interest rate (coupon) and the actual yield depends on the issue price. In the first loan, the price of 103.95% (above par value of 100%) lowers the yield to 0.595%. In the second, the price of 98.25% (below par) slightly increases the yield to 0.560%, partially compensating for the low coupon.
### Who purchases Swiss federal loans
Purchasers of these securities include commercial banks, insurance companies, occupational pension funds (LPP/BVG), institutional investors and private savers with a conservative profile. Swiss pension funds — which manage workers' contributions for mandatory pension insurance — allocate a significant portion of their portfolio to Swiss government securities, perceived as free from insolvency risk and fundamental to ensure stable returns to generations of retirees.
### Implications for financial stability
High coverage ratios allow the Confederation to finance itself without raising the interest rates offered. This keeps federal financing costs low, reducing pressure on the state budget and allowing the allocation of resources to welfare programs, infrastructure and social security (AVS/AHV, AI/IV, subsidies). For retail savers, it means that Swiss government securities remain a reliable investment, even if with modest returns compared to previous historical periods.
### Indirect connection with private pension provision
Many Swiss people will not realize that their pension fund (LPP/BVG) or their contributions to the third pillar (3a) managed by financial institutions are indirectly exposed to these loans. When the Confederation issues bonds at stable rates, this helps maintain predictable returns in conservative portfolios, even if the effect is invisible in the short term.
## Useful planning tools To estimate your pension strategy, use the [pension planner](nav:pension) and the [pillar 3 simulator](nav:pillar3). ## How to invest and inform yourself about federal loans
If you are interested in understanding where the Confederation finances itself or evaluating where to allocate your savings, here are the resources and practical steps to guide you.
### Official access to data
All technical details and the calendar of future issues are available through the Federal Finance Office (EFV) at admin.ch. The portal provides: - Complete historical data on past issues and realized yields - ISIN numbers and technical specifications for each loan - Indicative calendars for future issues - Information on legal restrictions for selling and trading
### Purchase channels for retail savers
Swiss federal loans can be purchased through: 1. **Swiss commercial banks**: access during the award procedure (usually reserved for large investor clients, but banks often allow indirect access through funds) 2. Financial intermediaries authorized by FINMA: asset management companies and online banks 3. Trading platforms: Swiss and international secondary bond markets
Most retail savers access these securities indirectly, through low-risk Swiss bond funds, conservative mixed funds, or automatically in their occupational pension portfolios (LPP).
### Timeline and step-by-step
September 9, 2026: Award procedures launched for institutional investors September 23, 2026: Settlement of the two loans After September 23: Availability on the secondary market for ordinary purchases and sales
If you wish to explore investment options in quality Swiss bonds, your bank or financial advisor can offer you personalized scenarios based on your risk profile and time horizon.
### Plan your pension with awareness
The stability of Swiss government securities makes them the backbone of every conservative pension strategy. If you are planning your contributions to the [third pillar (3a)](nav:pillar3) or evaluating how to allocate your savings for retirement, it is useful to know that a share in Swiss government bonds guarantees predictable returns, even if modest. Use our [third pillar calculator](nav:pillar3) to estimate how much to contribute annually and our [pension planner](nav:pension) to forecast the amount of your combined AVS/AHV pension and accumulated capital.

item.title: Broadband in rural areas: CHF 730 million
item.description: The Federal Council approves a CHF 730 million programme for fast internet connections in rural areas. Involved cantons and municipalities from 2030 to 2037 with fibre optics and radio communication.
item.content:encoded:
## In brief - The Federal Council is investing 730 million CHF for broadband in rural areas - LSBL program of 8 years (2030-2037) with equal cost-sharing by cantons - At least 1 gigabit/second download: the national minimum standard
## Key facts - **What**: Federal broadband support program (LSBL) for rural residential and commercial buildings - When: Messages transmitted to Parliament; operational program 2030-2037 - Where: Swiss rural areas (municipalities on a voluntary basis, with cantonal participation required) - Who: Federal Council, DATEC (Albert Rösti, head of department) - Amount: 730 million CHF total (365 million Confederation, 365 million Cantons) - Speed: at least 1 gigabit per second in download
The Federal Council has decided to bridge the infrastructure gap in Swiss rural areas through a federal broadband support program. An investment of 730 million francs will be dedicated to expanding networks, with a stated objective: to guarantee fast fixed internet connections to all residential and commercial buildings, even where private providers do not find economic convenience. Albert Rösti, head of the Federal Department of Communications (DATEC), announced the details.
The program, provisionally named Law on Broadband Support (LSBL), provides equally distributed financing: the Confederation covers 365 million francs through a commitment credit for the years 2030-2037, while the Cantons pay the same amount. The constraint is clear: no municipality can receive federal funds without the commitment to co-financing from the relevant canton.
### Optical fiber infrastructure, with alternatives
The priority remains optical fiber. Where expansion costs prove excessive, the program also accepts connections via terrestrial radio communications. The speed standard is unequivocal: at least one gigabit per second in download. The Federal Council has clarified that federal contributions will be limited to funds actually necessary, avoiding project over-dimensioning. The municipalities concerned will have to submit a formal application.
The temporal structure is defined: the program lasts eight years (2030-2037); the Federal Council may extend it only once for a maximum of three additional years if resources remain unspent.
### Financing from mobile concessions
An important novelty concerns the source of federal financing. The 365 million will come from taxes derived from future mobile telephony concessions. It will therefore not be a diversion of ordinary budget, but income dedicated to the telecommunications sector. ### How the mechanism works: the role of the Cantons
The system of access to LSBL funds has a clear but binding structure. The first step is the cantonal decision: each Canton decides whether to join the program, participation remains voluntary. However, those who choose not to participate leave their municipalities without access to federal funding. It is a powerful incentive: to receive even a single federal franc, the Canton has no alternative but to co-finance to the established extent (50% of the total amount of the project).
This structure creates a clear procedural hierarchy: the Canton decides to join, undertakes to pay 50% of the total funding, the Municipality applies for access to funds, the Confederation disburses its 50% only if the Canton has entered the program. The practical consequence is that the Municipalities of non-adhering Cantons remain completely excluded. A binding cantonal decision therefore affects all the underlying administrative levels.
### Design priority: fiber vs. radiocommunication
The choice of infrastructure is not neutral. Fiber optics remains the gold standard: superior speed, stability, prospects for future upgrades. But it's also expensive. The government has recognised this reality and inserted a flexibility clause: where the expansion of fibre entails very high costs, alternatives can be used via terrestrial radiocommunication.

If your municipality is located in a rural area and wishes to benefit from the LSBL program, the process is straightforward but requires coordination between administrative levels.
First step: verification of cantonal status. Contact the competent cantonal administration (Department or Office of Energy, Infrastructure or Telecommunications, depending on the canton) and ask if the Canton has joined the LSBL program. If the answer is negative, your municipality does not have access to federal funds. If positive, proceed to the next step.
**Second step: territory evaluation**. The program finances residential and commercial buildings in areas where private providers do not find economic viability. If your area is already covered by private operators with adequate speed (≥1 gigabit/s), the project may not be eligible. If fast connections are lacking, continue.
Third step: application submission. The municipality formally submits an application to the competent cantonal entity. The request must indicate: territory to be covered, target buildings, proposed infrastructure (fiber optic vs. radio communication), cost estimate and implementation timeline.
Fourth step: federal evaluation. The Confederation evaluates whether the project meets technical standards (minimum speed 1 gigabit/s, reasonable costs, territory effectively lacking bandwidth). If approved, the municipality receives the federal share (50%) and the Canton receives its share (50%).
Fifth step: implementation. The municipality or designated operator implements the infrastructure within the approved timeline.
### Funding and Administrative Responsibility
The money is not an unconditional subsidy. Federal contributions are limited to the minimum necessary funds: the government wants to avoid project oversizing or inflated costs. A technical-economic analysis will be central to evaluating the application. The Canton has dual responsibility: it decides whether to participate (political choice) and co-finances 50% (fiscal responsibility). If a Canton decides not to participate, its municipalities are completely excluded without exceptions.
### Critical Deadlines and Planning
The program begins in 2030 and covers eight years (until 2037). If resources remain unused, an extension until 2040 is possible. For municipalities, this means: if you wish to access the funding, you must submit an application and obtain approval by 2037 (or until 2040 if the program is effectively extended). The window is broad, but not endless. Rural areas that delay planning risk permanently losing the opportunity.
To assess the economic impact of the project at the municipal level — for example, the exact amount of local investment required for 50% co-financing — you can use the [calculators for infrastructure and budget](nav:calculator). To compare specific costs between different technologies (fiber optic, radio communication), contact your competent cantonal Department directly or local network operators. The decision to join the LSBL program remains in the hands of the Cantons: if yours has already joined, the next step is to contact your municipality to evaluate concrete projects.

item.title: Swiss tour operators in difficulty: 5-10% drop in turnover
item.description: FSV estimates a 5-10% contraction in 2026 due to geopolitics, summer heat and the collapse of US visitors. Additional costs 2.3m CHF for emergency returns.
item.content:encoded:
## In a nutshell - FSV forecasts a 5-10% drop in turnover in 2026 for Swiss tour operators - Middle East conflict cost CHF 2.3 million in repatriations and modifications - US visitors plummeted by 17% in the first 6 months of 2026
## Key facts - **What**: Swiss tour operators face contraction in turnover due to geopolitics, heat, high prices - When: 2026; Q1-Q2 data show negative trend - Who: FSV (Swiss Travel Federation), director Andrea Beffa - Where: Switzerland; global impacts (USA, Middle East) - Amount: Expected decrease 5-10%; Middle East conflict costs CHF 2.3 million - Volumes: 1600 returnees, 20,000 customer requests, 3400 booking changes
The Swiss Travel Federation (FSV) forecasts a drop in turnover of between 5 and 10% for the entire year 2026. Behind this contraction weigh geopolitical uncertainties, a particularly hot summer that has curbed last-minute bookings, and a collapse in demand that touches the prices of tourist packages, making Swiss customers increasingly cautious.
The impact of the conflict in the Middle East has been particularly severe. FSV members handled more than 3,400 reservation changes, processed more than 20,000 customer requests from people who wanted to cancel or change the trip, and repatriated more than 1,600 travelers. These emergency interventions have generated additional costs of more than CHF 2.3 million.
### Uncertainty and personalised advice
is just ### Travel preferences and behavior of Swiss tourists
Swiss clientele is undergoing a paradigm shift. Although it maintains a constant interest in exotic destinations and quality tourism, economic prudence has prevailed over the desire for adventure. FSV data shows that the number of trips has decreased, but—in parallel—the quality of spending required by tourists remains high. In other words: the Swiss travel less, but prefer superior experiences and services when they decide to travel.
For autumn 2026, preferences focus on Greece, Cyprus, Majorca, Egypt and the Canary Islands. Tunisia emerges with significant growth, signaling a search for alternative and perhaps more affordable destinations compared to classic European attractions. In the winter period, medium-haul flights will maintain Egypt, Gran Canaria and Tenerife as reference destinations, while long-haul will be dominated by Mauritius, Maldives and Thailand—destinations offering controlled climate and a complete escape from European uncertainty.
### The Collapse of the American Market
The most alarming figure concerns the United States. In the first six months of 2026, departures from Switzerland to the USA fell by 17% compared to the same period in 2025. In absolute terms, only 120,000 Swiss reached American territory in this period. If this trend continues through the end of the year, approximately 300,000 departures from Switzerland to the USA are forecast for 2026, Beffa explained to the Awp agency. This would represent the lowest figure since 2007.
The situation had already deteriorated last year: in 2025, registered arrivals had been 361,000, already down 11% compared to 2024. Overall, since the beginning of the Trump presidency, the country has lost about a quarter of Swiss visitors. A loss of this magnitude highlights how political turbulence and perceptions of global security affect the Swiss population's travel decisions.
### Impact on Cost of Living and Package Prices
Tourist packages cost slightly more than last year, mainly due to inflation in services and currency volatility. This price increase has accelerated the aforementioned caution of Swiss clientele, creating a vicious cycle: more expensive → fewer bookings → tour operators who must optimize margins with more selective clients. To explore further how tourism inflation impacts the [cost of living in Switzerland](nav:cost-of-living), consult our dedicated analyses.

For Swiss tour operators and travel agencies, the FSV's message is clear: competition is played out on the quality of advice and the ability to offer personalized packages that reduce the perceived risk for the client. Agencies that know how to guide tourists through alternative destinations—Tunisia, Cyprus, Southeast Asia with a focus on Maldives and Thailand—will be able to maintain acceptable margins even in a context of reduced volumes.
For individual travelers, caution remains golden. Anyone who still wishes to travel in the last months of 2026 should contact FSV-associated agencies directly to obtain professional advice on managing geopolitical risks, prefer destinations with a historical reputation for stability (Mediterranean destinations, established Southeast Asia), and carefully verify modification and cancellation conditions in their packages.
### Perspectives for 2027
The trend could stabilize in 2027, but it will depend on the global geopolitical landscape. Pressure on tourism service prices will continue as long as uncertainty persists. For those working in the sector—guides, operators, hotel partners, transport—these volume declines bring pressure on employment and income. [Jobs in Swiss tourism](nav:jobs) will suffer from the contraction until demand returns to historical levels.
### How to prepare for the coming months
If you are planning a trip for autumn or winter, contact an FSV agency right away. The last months of the year will be full of surprises—geopolitical changes, last-minute offers, group cancellations that free up spots. Agencies with experienced consultants will be able to help you find the best compromise between price, quality, and perceived security.
To measure the economic impact of these changes on your family or work situation, our [salary calculator](nav:calculator) offers budget scenarios for various European and international destinations—useful for assessing how the new landscape of package prices could affect your travel capacity. item.description: A new alliance of economic actors supports the energy agreement with the EU. Switzerland depends on winter imports and exports in summer.
